title: Ὄνος ἵππον μακαρίζων
titleEn: The Donkey Counting the Horse Blessed
part: The Donkey Counting the Horse Blessed (Chambry 268 · Perry 357)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 268 (= Perry 357). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος ἵππον ἐμακάριζεν, ὡς ἀφθόνως τρεφόμενον καὶ ἐπιμελῶς, αὐτὸς μηδ’ ἀχύρων ἅλις ἔχων, καὶ ταῦτα πλεῖστα ταλαιπωρῶν.
sentences.tr: Onos hippon emakarizen, hōs aphthonōs trephomenon kai epimelōs, autos mēd’ achyrōn halis echōn, kai tauta pleista talaipōrōn.
sentences.l: A donkey was counting a horse blessed, as being fed lavishly and carefully, while he himself did not have even chaff enough, and that though toiling very greatly.
sentences.i: A donkey called a horse fortunate, seeing him fed lavishly and looked after, when he himself had not even chaff enough — and that for all his hard labour.
sentences.n: ὡς with a participle gives the ground as the speaker sees it: this is the donkey's reason, not the narrator's. καὶ ταῦτα, 'and that too', is the regular Greek for adding a concession, and πλεῖστα is an adverbial accusative, 'very greatly'. μηδέ rather than οὐδέ because the participle ἔχων is felt as a condition.

sentences.t: Ἐπεὶ δὲ καιρὸς ἐπέστη πολέμου, καὶ ὁ στρατιώτης ἔνοπλος ἀνέβη τὸν ἵππον, πανταχόσε τοῦτον ἐλαύνων, καὶ δὴ καὶ μέσον τῶν πολεμίων εἰσήλασε, καὶ ὁ ἵππος πληγεὶς ἔκειτο.
sentences.tr: Epei de kairos epestē polemou, kai ho stratiōtēs enoplos anebē ton hippon, pantachose touton elaunōn, kai dē kai meson tōn polemiōn eisēlase, kai ho hippos plēgeis ekeito.
sentences.l: But when the hour of war came on, and the soldier in his armour mounted the horse, driving him in every direction, and indeed drove him into the middle of the enemy, then the horse, struck, lay there.
sentences.i: But when war came on, and the soldier in his armour mounted the horse and rode him this way and that, and at the last drove him into the thick of the enemy, the horse took a wound and lay there.
sentences.n: ἐπέστη, 'stood over', is the regular verb for what comes upon a man unbidden — a dream, a god, or here the hour of war. ἀναβαίνω takes a plain accusative of the horse mounted. καὶ δὴ καί marks the last and worst step of a series. ἔκειτο, 'was lying', is the Greek way of saying he was down and did not get up. The ἐπεί clause runs on through three coordinated verbs before the sentence reaches its main clause at ὁ ἵππος πληγεὶς ἔκειτο — the pile-up is the battle.

sentences.t: Ταῦτα ἑωρακὼς ὁ ὄνος τὸν ἵππον μεταβαλλόμενος ἐταλάνιζεν.
sentences.tr: Tauta heōrakōs ho onos ton hippon metaballomenos etalanizen.
sentences.l: Having seen these things, the donkey, changing round, was counting the horse wretched.
sentences.i: Having seen this, the donkey changed his mind and called the horse wretched instead.
sentences.n: ταλανίζω is the exact opposite of the μακαρίζω of the first line — to pronounce a man wretched — and the fable is built on the pair. μεταβαλλόμενος is middle: he turns himself round, shifts his own position.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὐ δεῖ τοὺς ἄρχοντας καὶ πλουσίους ζηλοῦν, ἀλλὰ τὸν κατ’ ἐκείνων φθόνον καὶ τὸν κίνδυνον ἀναλογιζομένους τὴν πενίαν ἀγαπᾶν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ou dei tous archontas kai plousious zēloun, alla ton kat’ ekeinōn phthonon kai ton kindynon analogizomenous tēn penian agapan.
sentences.l: The fable shows that one must not envy rulers and the rich, but, reckoning up the ill-will directed against them and the danger, must be content with poverty.
sentences.n: κατά with the genitive is hostile, so the φθόνος is the grudge others bear them, not the grudge they bear. ἀγαπάω here is not passion but acceptance — to be satisfied with what one has. The accusative ἀναλογιζομένους agrees with the unexpressed subject of the infinitives governed by δεῖ.
